title: Flip the interposer: wafer-scale DRAM becomes the substrate
idea: Reverse the substrate role: instead of a passive silicon interposer carrying GPU and HBM side by side, a full 300 mm DRAM wafer (cell arrays plus a top hybrid-bond layer) is the substrate, and compute chiplets are hybrid-bonded face-down onto it at ~9 um pitch so each chiplet sits directly over its own memory tiles. Global chiplet-to-chiplet wiring runs in the DRAM wafer's upper metals.
why: Removes the passive interposer and HBM TSV stacks (facts 5, 6): micrometre vertical paths at ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, and ~3x less wafer area per bit than HBM because there are no TSV keep-outs; tile-level redundancy absorbs wafer defects.

title: DRAM-bridge: the chiplet bridge die is itself memory
idea: Rearrange the bridge's role: the small embedded silicon bridges (EMIB/LSI-style) that link adjacent GPU chiplets are fabricated as DRAM dies whose top metals carry the die-to-die wires and whose array area is dual-ported to both neighbouring chiplets' edge bumps. Silicon that today only carries wires becomes a shared buffer between neighbours.
why: A 16 mm2 bridge at ~0.3 Gb/mm2 holds ~0.6 GB, so 8 bridges add ~5 GB of on-package shared memory at <0.5 pJ/bit with zero extra package area; chiplets exchange tensors through memory instead of the link (fact 5).

title: Carousel DRAM: memory broadcasts everything, consumers just listen
idea: Reverse request/response: in carousel mode the DRAM runs a fixed scan that reads every row in order and broadcasts it on a wide unidirectional bus, and consumers (e.g. LLM decode cores that read the same weights in the same order every token) latch what they need. The scan read restores each row, so separate refresh disappears, and there is no command/address bus or random activation; a small conventional port handles writes.
why: Attacks overfetch and refresh (facts 3, 5, 8): 100% row utilisation instead of ~1/128, refresh energy and bandwidth folded into useful reads, CA pins and controller removed; estimated 3-5x lower pJ per useful bit for weight streaming.

title: Laser in the host, mirror in the memory: optical backscatter
idea: Reverse who emits light: the accelerator package holds the only laser and sends continuous-wave light to each DRAM stack, where reflective electro-absorption modulators on the base die encode read data onto the returning beam, like RFID backscatter. The DRAM side has no laser, no transmitter thermal tuning and no high-power driver.
why: Data-movement energy and reach (fact 5): DRAM-side link energy ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit, and memory can sit 10-100 cm away so capacity is no longer capped by HBM beachfront; the hot memory stack is free of laser-reliability problems.

title: Transpose in the base die: return columns, not rows
idea: Rearrange data order at the stack boundary: a small SRAM corner-turn buffer in the HBM base die gathers strided elements (e.g. one head's slice across many tokens of a KV cache) from open rows in many banks and packs them into dense column-major bursts, so the link carries only the bytes requested.
why: Overfetch and link energy (facts 5, 8): for strided or sparse access, link bytes and pJ fall 2-8x because waste is discarded on-stack, millimetres from the array, instead of after crossing the PHY.

title: Fewer, faster TSVs: serialize 16:1 inside the stack
idea: Reverse HBM's many-slow-wires rule inside the stack: each TSV carries a 16:1 serialized 25-32 Gb/s stream from compact injection-locked transceivers on each die, cutting signal TSVs from thousands to a few hundred at a relaxed 40-50 um pitch.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV area and keep-out shrink ~80% and the relaxed pitch raises stack yield; costs ~0.3 pJ/bit of SerDes energy, so it suits capacity-oriented stacks rather than peak-bandwidth ones.

title: Stack untested dies, route around failures with a base-die crossbar
idea: Reverse test-then-stack: stack 14 lightly tested dies for a 12-die product and put a channel crossbar in the base die that maps logical channels onto whichever dies and channels pass final package test, set by fuses. Yield comes from routing around defects rather than from known-good-die screening.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): ~14% die over-provisioning lifts stack yield from ~70% to >95% and removes a costly wafer-level test insertion.

title: Accumulate-on-write: the host sends sums, never reads back
idea: Reverse read-modify-write ownership: the interface gains an 'add' write command, and the HBM base die does the read, the BF16/FP32 add and the write-back next to the array, so gradient accumulation, optimizer moments and KV updates never cross the link twice.
why: Halves link traffic in accumulation-heavy training phases, ~30-50% of optimizer-step bytes (fact 5), and lets ECC be recomputed locally.

title: Return addresses, not data: similarity search inside the stack
idea: Reverse the query direction: the host sends a query vector, a dot-product/top-k engine in the base die scans stored keys at internal bandwidth, and it returns only the k indices and scores; the host then fetches just those k values.
why: Long-context KV caches and vector databases (facts 5, 8): link traffic drops 10-100x because keys never leave the stack.

title: Bit-plane-major storage with progressive-precision fetch
idea: Rearrange bit order: weights are stored transposed so that each DRAM burst holds the same bit position of 512 different weights. The accelerator fetches the top 4 bit-planes first and fetches lower planes only for layers or tokens whose error estimate needs them.
why: Facts 5 and 8: inference moves 2-4x fewer bytes on average at near-equal accuracy, multiplying effective bandwidth and turning precision into a runtime knob instead of a stored format.

title: Lane-direction-reconfigurable PHY for read-heavy phases
idea: Reverse fixed DQ symmetry: each lane has a transmitter and a receiver at both ends and can be reassigned in microseconds, so during LLM decode ~90% of lanes point memory-to-host and they flip back for checkpoint writes; per-burst bus turnaround disappears.
why: Recovers the ~10-15% bandwidth lost to read/write turnarounds and gives up to ~1.8x effective read bandwidth in read-dominated phases (fact 5).

title: Adiabatic resonant links that recycle wire charge every cycle
idea: Reverse dissipate-and-replace signalling: each interposer line's capacitance forms an LC tank with an on-die spiral or package inductor, and data is encoded by phase or selective clamping of the resonant swing, so most of the CV^2 energy sloshes back instead of burning in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data-movement energy (facts 5, 10): 3-5x lower energy on long interposer and substrate lines (~0.5 vs ~2 pJ/bit), at the cost of fixed-frequency operation.

title: Compute on top, memory underneath, power through the stack
idea: Reverse HBM's placement: the accelerator die sits on top of a DRAM stack next to the heat sink, dense power-TSV columns through every DRAM die feed it, and the memory interface becomes a direct face-to-back hybrid bond into the top DRAM die.
why: Removes interposer beachfront and HBM PHYs (facts 5, 6): ~10 TB/s per cm2 of vertical bandwidth at ~0.1 pJ/bit, and the usual memory-on-logic thermal problem is avoided because logic sits next to the cooler.

title: Backside signal highway on the DRAM die
idea: Reverse backside power delivery: after thinning, put thick low-RC copper on the DRAM die backside for the global data and command buses, connected by nano-TSVs to each bank's local I/O, which frees front-side metal for array wiring and shrinks the periphery's routing channels.
why: Facts 5 and 7: on-die global data-line energy, a large slice of the 3-4 pJ/bit, drops 2-3x on thick wires, and periphery routing area falls ~10%.

title: Package lid as a sub-THz broadcast waveguide
idea: Reverse the heat spreader's role: the copper lid and a substrate ground plane form a parallel-plate waveguide, and each chiplet has a slot antenna radiating 100-300 GHz into it, so one memory chiplet can broadcast a read to many compute chiplets at once without routed wires.
why: Multicast data movement (fact 5): one transmission serves N receivers for weight broadcast, and substrate routing layers are freed.

title: Data over the power network inside the HBM stack
idea: Rearrange power and signal roles: superimpose low-amplitude, high-frequency data on the many power/ground TSVs (which outnumber signal TSVs) using AC coupling and band separation above the PDN resonance, turning idle PDN capacity into extra channels.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): up to 30-50% more effective I/O with no added TSVs; the risk is PDN noise coupling into the array.

title: Memory-centric motherboard: compute cartridges plug into memory
idea: Reverse socket roles: the board is a mesh of DRAM modules and CXL/optical switches, and CPUs and accelerators are pluggable cartridges that attach to the memory regions they need. Memory stays installed for 8-10 years while compute is refreshed every 2.
why: Raises usable supply by ending DRAM disposal at each server refresh and recovering ~25-40% stranded DRAM, effectively 1.5-2x more usable bits from the same production.

title: Sense amps on the host: bitline-pitch bonding across dies
idea: Rearrange array and periphery: the DRAM die carries only cell arrays whose bitline segments end in hybrid-bond pads, and sense amplifiers, decoders and I/O live on a logic-process die bonded below at ~1 um pitch. The DRAM process loses its periphery steps, and fast logic transistors sense at lower voltage.
why: Fact 7 (periphery ~49% of die): the array die gets nearly 2x bits per mm2; logic-node sense amps lower VARY and energy (fact 10); one logic die can serve two array dies.

title: Pulse-position signalling: four bits per single edge
idea: Reverse amplitude-based encoding: each lane sends exactly one edge per symbol window, and that edge's position among 16 time slots carries 4 bits, read by a shared time-to-digital converter, so the wire toggles once per 4 bits instead of about twice.
why: CV^2 link energy (facts 5, 10): 3-4x fewer transitions on capacitive interposer wires gives 50-70% lower link energy at moderate data rates.

title: Optical vias through solid silicon, no holes drilled
idea: Reverse drill-then-fill: instead of copper TSVs, thinned DRAM dies (silicon is transparent at 1.3-1.55 um) pass data vertically as light from bonded III-V micro-emitters to Ge photodiodes on dies above, with each tier on its own wavelength so beams cross intermediate dies unabsorbed.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out, copper-extrusion stress or Cu fill, and dies can be oxide-bonded; ~0.5 pJ/bit target.

title: Sell DRAM as bondable wafers and let customers stack
idea: Reverse the HBM value chain: memory makers sell finished DRAM wafers with a published hybrid-bond pad standard, and foundries, OSATs and accelerator firms do the thinning, stacking and base-die integration themselves, creating many parallel HBM assembly lines.
why: Capital intensity and U.S. manufacturability: the HBM bottleneck moves from three memory makers' packaging lines to any advanced packager, including U.S. OSATs.

title: Memory as master: the stack pushes tensors to compute
idea: Reverse who initiates: the host writes a descriptor program (tensor shapes, strides, schedule) once, and a DMA engine in the DRAM base die pushes data on its own schedule into the accelerator's SRAM over a write-only link; the host never issues per-line reads.
why: Removes request traffic and round-trip latency, and memory can order row activations optimally (fewer activations, less energy and row-hammer exposure); ~20% more effective bandwidth (facts 5, 8, 9).

title: Wire-rich, clock-poor: 100k-wire interface at 200 MHz
idea: Push narrow-fast to the opposite extreme, wide-slow: hybrid-bond 100,000+ data pads between memory and logic at 3 um pitch, each a plain full-swing CMOS wire at 0.4 V and ~200 MHz with no SerDes, DLL, termination or equalisation.
why: Fact 5: ~0.02-0.05 pJ/bit and 20+ Tb/s per stack, with PHY area near zero (fact 7).

title: Upcycle commodity DRAM dies with pad-rearranging RDL
idea: Rearrange the pads, not the die: buy known-good LPDDR bare dies, and in a university nanofab add a polyimide plus electroplated-Cu redistribution layer (contact aligner, 5 um lines) that fans the edge pad row into an area array matched to a logic test chip, then flip-chip the two face-to-face.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: wide-I/O-like short links from commodity dies with ~$1M of tools, showing ~1 pJ/bit without a TSV line (facts 5, 6).

title: Bookshelf stack: dies stand on edge in an etched rack
idea: Rotate the stack 90 degrees: thin dies are diced, given sidewall pads by angled shadow-mask evaporation over the edge, and inserted vertically into a DRIE-etched silicon rack whose trench floors carry solder pads, so every die connects straight to the base with no TSVs and no die-to-die relay.
why: TSV tax eliminated (fact 6): each die gets its own edge bus (hundreds of I/O at 20 um pitch), and dies cool from both faces with fluid flowing between them.

title: Inductive broadcast stack: one coil talks to all tiers
idea: Replace through-vias with through-fields: plate 2-turn spiral coils in the RDL of thinned (<=25 um) dies stacked with adhesive; a base-die transmitter coil couples to aligned coils on every tier at once, so commands broadcast to all dies and each die replies in its own time slot.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV etch or Cu fill, ~0.1-0.2 pJ/bit inductive links, made with plating and adhesive bonding only.

title: Bumpless capacitive face-to-face: the passivation is the link
idea: Reverse 'remove the dielectric to connect': leave the 0.5-1 um passivation intact, use 5 um pads on each die as coupling capacitors, and align the dies face-to-face with an adhesive; pulse-mode receivers detect the coupled edges, so no UBM, solder or CMP-grade hybrid-bond surface is needed.
why: Capital and yield: 5-10 um-pitch vertical links with only lithography and a flip-chip aligner, ~0.1 pJ/bit, and tolerance to particles that kill hybrid bonds (facts 5, 6).

title: Photonic wire bonds written after chips are placed
idea: Reverse align-then-place: place memory-side and host-side photonic dies coarsely (+-10 um), image their couplers, and write freeform polymer waveguides between them by two-photon lithography, so the link adapts to placement error rather than demanding sub-micron alignment.
why: Optical memory links (fact 5) without active alignment, a dominant cost of co-packaged optics; university fabs with two-photon writers can prototype memory-disaggregation links.

title: Double-sided glass interposer: memory below, compute above
idea: Flip the interposer into a sandwich: make through-glass vias in photostructurable glass by UV exposure, bake and HF etch, bond DRAM dies to the underside and compute to the top directly above them, so the memory path is a 100-200 um vertical via instead of millimetres of lateral wire.
why: Facts 5 and 6: lateral interposer wires become short verticals (~0.2 pJ/bit), and glass is cheaper than a silicon interposer and needs only basic litho and wet etch.

title: Fluidic self-assembly of shape-keyed memory tiles
idea: Reverse pick-and-place: diced memory tiles with keyed asymmetric outlines tumble in a fluid over a logic wafer etched with matching recesses, and the capillary pull of molten low-temperature solder in each recess drags tiles into ~1 um alignment, assembling thousands in parallel.
why: Capital intensity of placement and bonding tools; parallel assembly makes many small, high-yield memory tiles economical.

title: Transfer-print thin memory membranes, then wire them lithographically
idea: Reverse bond-then-connect: undercut-release memory chiplets into <10 um membranes, pick them with a PDMS stamp onto the logic wafer, planarize with BCB, and pattern vias and copper across both with ordinary lithography, giving a monolithic-like 2-3 um-pitch connection with no bumps.
why: Fact 5: interconnect density ~10x microbumps at ~0.05 pJ/bit, using university-standard transfer printing, spin coating and plating.

title: Alignment-free z-axis film from anodized-alumina nanowires
idea: Reverse 'align pad to pad': anodize a porous alumina film (~100 nm pores at 200 nm pitch), electroplate copper nanowires through it, and laminate it between memory and logic dies; any pad overlap connects through many parallel nanowires while the alumina insulates laterally, so pitch is set by pad size, not alignment accuracy.
why: Capital: ~5 um-pitch vertical links with coarse +-2 um aligners; anodization and plating are beaker-level processes.

title: One via through the whole stack, etched last
idea: Reverse via-first-per-die: adhesive-bond 4-8 thinned dies that each reserve aligned keep-out windows, then DRIE a single hole through the entire stack, line it with parylene and fill copper once, contacting each die through exposed sidewall metal rings.
why: TSV tax and process count (fact 6): one via process instead of one per die and fewer bonded interfaces in the signal path; DRIE plus plating suffices.

title: Active glass interposer with oxide-TFT repeaters
idea: Move the PHY into the substrate: build low-temperature IGZO thin-film-transistor repeaters, multiplexers and charge-recycling drivers directly on a glass interposer (sputter plus contact litho, <350 C), so memory and compute dies use tiny low-swing pads and the interposer regenerates signals over centimetres.
why: Fact 7: strips much PHY area from DRAM dies, and memory can sit further from compute for more capacity at ~0.5 pJ/bit; TFT-on-glass is a university process.

title: Test first, wire last: liquid-metal rewiring of good dies
idea: Reverse wire-then-test: mount dies on a substrate under PDMS microchannels, and after electrical test inject gallium-indium liquid metal only into channels that join good dies and good channels to the host, then seal, so defective dies are simply never connected.
why: Yield and capital for multi-die memory modules, without known-good-die test cost; PDMS soft lithography is basic, best for wide buses at <=1 GHz.

title: University nanofab packaging commons with an open bonding PDK
idea: Reverse the innovation order: fund a network of ~10 university nanofabs with a shared open PDK for RDL, glass interposers and die-to-die bonding on purchased commodity DRAM dies, so startups prototype memory packaging in months before any commercial line exists.
why: U.S. manufacturability and time: builds a domestic packaging and integration share and workforce on top of ~1-2% U.S. DRAM output, and de-risks processes for <$50M/yr.

title: Origami memory: fold a flex ribbon of dies over compute
idea: Rearrange a planar layout into a fold: bond thinned memory dies to a parylene or polyimide flex with litho-patterned 5 um copper traces, then fold it accordion-style so the dies stack above the compute die while their wiring runs around the folds instead of through the silicon.
why: TSV-free 3D stacking with <5 mm links (fact 6), each die keeping its own traces; flex fabrication is standard in university cleanrooms.

title: Cool from inside: microchannels etched into memory die backsides
idea: Reverse the heat path so memory can sit on top of compute: DRIE ~100 um microchannels into the back of each die, seal them with the next bonded layer, and circulate dielectric coolant through the stack so heat leaves sideways instead of through the hot logic.
why: Removes the thermal limit on memory-on-logic stacking and HBM stack height, enabling 16+ high stacks with vertical links (facts 5, 6).

title: Air-gap transmission lines by sacrificial polymer release
idea: Reverse 'more dielectric': pattern interposer signal lines on a sacrificial polymer (e.g. polynorbornene) and thermally decompose it through a porous cap, leaving copper lines suspended in air (k~1) instead of polyimide (k~3.3).
why: CV^2 link energy (facts 5, 10): line capacitance roughly halves, giving ~2x lower energy and faster interposer memory links with spin, pattern and bake steps only.

title: Microspring sockets for reworkable, upgradable memory dies
idea: Reverse permanent bonding: sputter stress-graded metal fingers that curl up off the interposer into 20 um-pitch microsprings, and clamp memory dies onto them, so dies can be tested, swapped or carried to the next compute generation after assembly.
why: Yield and supply: bad or worn dies are replaced instead of scrapping a whole ~$10k package, and DRAM is reused across compute generations; stressed-metal springs need only sputtering and a release etch.

title: Optical clock broadcast from above, no clock pins
idea: Reverse forwarded-clock wiring: one modulated LED or laser illuminates the package through a window, and silicon photodiodes on every memory and logic die recover the same clock edge simultaneously, removing clock trees, DLLs and clock bumps from the memory interface.
why: Clocking is ~20-40% of PHY energy; a skew-free global clock shrinks PHY area (fact 7) and link energy (fact 5); photodiodes and windows are simple uni-fab structures.

title: Coaxial microbumps: two signals per bump, self-shielded
idea: Rearrange the bump: plate a core pillar, coat it with conformal ALD or parylene dielectric, then plate a ring shell, giving a coaxial bump whose core carries one signal and whose shell carries ground or a second signal.
why: Facts 5 and 6: doubles signal density at the same pitch (or allows relaxed pitch), and the shielding cuts crosstalk at 10+ Gb/s; plating and ALD are university staples.

title: Cryogenic copper interposer at 77 K for memory packages
idea: Reverse room-temperature design: run the memory package in liquid nitrogen, where copper resistivity falls ~7x and DRAM retention rises by orders of magnitude, and draw interposer lines 7x narrower or longer so more memory dies connect at the same pJ/bit.
why: Refresh nearly vanishes (fact 3) and low-RC lines enable long low-swing links (fact 5); the university fab builds the fine-line interposer, but cooling overhead (~10x at 77 K) must be paid back by data-centre-scale integration.

title: Move decoupling off the DRAM die into the interposer
idea: Rearrange where charge reservoirs live: deposit high-k ALD (HfO2/ZrO2) MIM or deep-trench capacitors in the interposer directly under each memory die's power bumps, so the DRAM die can drop most of its on-die decap.
why: Fact 7: on-die decap is several percent of the DRAM periphery; ~uF/cm2 interposer decap frees that area for bits; ALD and DRIE are routine uni-fab steps.

title: Silicon ribbon sub-THz waveguides between memory and compute
idea: Reverse 'metal for wires': DRIE-etch high-resistivity silicon ribbons on the interposer as dielectric waveguides for 150-300 GHz carriers, with tapered couplers at each chiplet, giving low-loss 100+ Gb/s channels over several centimetres without copper skin-effect loss.
why: Memory can sit 5-20 cm away for capacity beyond beachfront at ~1 pJ/bit (fact 5); the waveguides are plain silicon etch.

title: Power by light, data by wire: photovoltaic-fed memory dies
idea: Swap delivery roles: a laser delivers power through a window or fibre onto photovoltaic cells on the top die of a memory stack, so the power TSVs that today outnumber signal TSVs can be repurposed for data.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): frees ~40-60% of TSVs; only viable for low-power capacity stacks (<=0.5 W) because PV conversion is ~50%; PV cells and windows are uni-fab buildable.
